episode.throughLine: After refusals at home and abroad, a woman signs the risk contract, continues training after a pupil's death, qualifies, and returns with more people still to help.

contentProfile.contentNote: Racial and gender discrimination; a student dies in an aviation accident, described without physical detail.

facts.statement: Coleman was born in 1892 and was about twenty-nine during her 1920–1921 training in France.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening biography: born in Atlanta, Texas, in 1892; license date 15 June 1921.

facts.statement: According to her sister Elois, American aviation schools rejected Coleman because she was Black, and sometimes also because she was a woman.

sourceRefs.locator: Smithsonian packet pp. 7–8, quoted Brave Bessie excerpt beginning 'She was refused'.

facts.statement: Her sister recalled that Coleman took the problem to Robert Abbott, enrolled in a language school on his advice, and received help contacting a French aviation school.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet pp. 7–8, quoted passage beginning 'She took her quest'.

facts.statement: Coleman took French classes, saved and sought sponsors, then crossed to Europe in November 1920.
Coleman said the first French school she approached would not take women after two women had died; she went to another school.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 19, Not Satisfied Yet, paragraph from 'I first went to Paris' through 'another school'.

facts.statement: Coleman said she signed a school contract accepting responsibility and risk to her own life.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 20, Better to Fly High, paragraph beginning 'When you first enter'.

facts.statement: Coleman said she wanted Black people represented in aviation and wanted to encourage others to learn.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 19, opening paragraph, account of why she learned to fly.

facts.statement: Coleman said she saw a pupil killed during her training and experienced a shock to her nerves.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 20, Better to Fly High, 'In school I saw a pupil killed instantly' through 'my nerves'.

facts.statement: In the same account Coleman said she retained her nerve and continued after the pupil's death.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 20, Better to Fly High, continuation after 'my nerves'.

facts.statement: Coleman recalled walking to school each day to finish her course.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 20, Better to Fly High, final paragraph on walking; disputed mileage/duration not adopted.

facts.statement: Coleman said she finished the course, took the examination, passed, and kept flying to improve.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 19, Not Satisfied Yet, 'There I finished my course' through 'perfect myself'.

facts.statement: The FAI granted Coleman her pilot's licence on 15 June 1921.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraph and paragraph beginning 'After booking'.

facts.statement: Coleman said she later took further lessons at another school near Paris under a pilot she described as an ace.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 19, Not Satisfied Yet, 'Later, I left the school' through lessons under an ace.

facts.statement: A contemporary report dated New York, 25 September 1921, announced Coleman's return from aviation study in France.

sourceRefs.locator: Morning Oregonian, 26 September 1921, p. 4, brief headed Negress Now Aviatrix.

facts.statement: A Chicago Defender reporter visited Coleman at her home after her return; she spoke about training and offered information to people interested in aviation.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 19 opening and p. 20 closing sentence.

facts.statement: At that interview Coleman said she would not be satisfied until other Black people could fly.

sourceRefs.locator: Packet p. 19, Not Satisfied Yet, first sentence.

facts.statement: Coleman was the first African American woman to receive a pilot's licence.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraph on the 15 June 1921 licence.

facts.statement: Coleman died in an aircraft accident in 1926.

sourceRefs.locator: Closing paragraphs, account of 30 April 1926 flight and death; detail omitted.
Packet p. 19, opening paragraph, final sentence of Coleman's answer about why she learned to fly.

arc.canonicalText: She was at a flying school abroad, signing a contract. She was about twenty-nine. In her account, the paper made her responsible for the risk to her life. The school did not take responsibility for her life. She signed. She had come from another country to learn to fly. Before the crossing, she had taken language classes and saved money. Other people had helped pay for the trip. Now the training required her own agreement to its risks.
arc.sourceNote: The school-contract scene is her retrospective 1921 account, marked probable. No desk, pen, bodily gesture, or instant emotional interpretation is supplied. The actual signing date is not recorded.

arc.canonicalText: At the school, she saw another student killed. The death shocked her nerves. She had signed a paper accepting danger to herself. Now someone learning the same work had died. The danger belonged to the lessons she had come to take. She was still a student there.
arc.sourceNote: The primary account supports the witnessed death and shock, but not its date, a relationship with the pupil, or a developed interior sequence. HOLD for craft: this low point cannot currently sustain the prescribed full scene without repetition or invented particulars.

arc.canonicalText: She continued her training. She said that her nerve held and she kept going. Her course still involved going to school. She walked there as part of the work of learning. She wanted to finish the course.
arc.sourceNote: HOLD for moment specificity: the interview documents continued training but no dated next flight, particular lesson, or immediate return. The prose deliberately makes no next-day or continuous-scene claim.

arc.canonicalText: Getting into this school had already taken more than one attempt. The first school she approached abroad had refused to accept women. It had lost two women who were learning to fly. She had gone to a different school. Rejection had also shaped the route that brought her overseas. In her sister's recollection, schools at home refused her because she was Black. Some also refused her because she was a woman. She took the problem to a newspaper publisher who helped her. On his advice, she enrolled in a language school. He also helped her contact a school abroad. After all that, there were still lessons and the walk to school.
arc.sourceNote: Explicit backward-looking compression gives the prior failures; it does not place these rejections after the pupil's death. Sister's evidence is later recollection and marked probable. Do not generalize one French refusal into universal policy.

arc.canonicalText: She took the school's examination and passed. She had completed the training that followed the signed contract. A pilot's licence was issued to her. The paper recorded that she had qualified. Passing did not mark the end of her lessons. She kept flying to improve. Then she went to another school for further instruction. In her remembered account, the teacher was an experienced pilot. She was still taking lessons.
arc.sourceNote: HOLD for craft: examination result and continued lessons are supported, but no exact test manoeuvre, location within the field, or immediate action during the exam was established. This passage compresses the documented sequence; it must not be called a fully shaped single moment.

arc.canonicalText: She returned home as a licensed pilot. A reporter visited her there to ask about flying. She explained the training and the contract. She also spoke about people who had not had her chance. She wanted more Black people to be able to fly. Her own licence had not completed that work. She offered to share information about aviation and its schools. The article told interested people they could see her. She could answer questions about the course. Looking back, she said: “I tried and was successful.”
arc.sourceNote: September–October 1921 return and home interview. Does not import her later fatal accident into this episode's ending or claim she opened a school. The later death appears in the fold.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Bessie Coleman.

She was the first African American woman to earn a pilot's licence. Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you. You are allowed to want something without knowing the whole way toward it. You do not have to feel fearless.
arc.sourceNote: The reveal uses the museum's documented distinction; no inspirational comparison or directive.

dramatizationLimits: No invented rejection office, classroom, flight sequence, crash description, witness dialogue, or emotional recovery.
Near-contemporary interview is a remembered account, not a transcript of the events.
Do not use the conflicting nine-mile/ten-month numbers or the newspaper's incorrect age as settled fact.
HOLD: current primary detail does not establish a located next flight or examination scene.
avoidRules: No name, year, city, institution or distinctive aircraft model before the bridge.
Do not say that she resumed flying the next day, completed ten months in seven, or opened her own school.
Do not call the licence proof that racism disappeared or promise similar results to readers.
